Paragraph 717 of the existing or old law-
This has reference to the proposed United States tariff regulations or revisions.
Paragraph 717 if the existing or old law, imposes a duty of 2 cents a pound on "fish, fresh, frozen or packed in ice-such as halibut, salmon, mackerel and swordfish," with one cent a pound on other fish "not specially provided for".
The new bill keeps substantially the same rates but adds a provision for 2J cents a pound on fish which is filleted, skinned, boned, sliced or divided into portions. It also provides for 2J cents a pound on dried and unsalted fish, of cod, haddock, hake, pollock, and eusk and If cents on other dried and unsealed fish.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
sat last we were considering vote 133, and were dealing with the following item:
Tabusintac-wharf extension, $3,000.

There were one or two
questions asked by my hon. friends which I promised to answer. One question was asked by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLarem) in connection with Lomeville. The hon. member asked why the total appropriation of $11,300 had1 not been fully expended. I have looked into this matter and I find that the estimate of the cost of removing 11,250 oubic yards, scow measurement, was $1 per yard, and it was estimated that that work would take up the whole of the appropriation. Whether the engineer's estimate was high or whether the contract price which we got for the work was low, we were able to have the work done at 65 cents per cubic yard, with the result that the total expenditure for removing very nearly that amount of material only came to about 65 per cent of what we had anticipated. I am told that it is probable that some work will be done the cost of which will come out of the general vote.

I pointed out to the
minister that the work had been found to be incomplete and not carried out to such an extent as to enable the work to serve the purpose for which it was intended, to make a safe refuge from heavy weather. The minister stated that he would read the report of the engineer, and I had hoped that the engineer would be recommending that some further work be done.
'Mr. Cardin.]

In the latter part of December, before the work was completed, a report was made by the engineer, and if my memory serves me aright that was the last report we received. He said, he would probably ask for a further amount to complete this next year, but apparently there has been no further request from him. I would call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the actual dredging done was within 115 cubic yards of the 11,250 cubic yards which had been estimated and for which the appropriation was made last year.

Do I understand the
minister to say that he expects to make arrangements to continue the work and complete it?

I would not say to complete it, but further work is going to be done and I expect that it will be provided for out of the general vote. Since the hon. member asked the question the other evening I have inquired into this matter, and I have the engineer's report of September 22, reading as follows:
Your letter of 30th July, authorizing dredging to be undertaken by Mr. James S. Gregory at Lorneville. I have to report this dreging was begun on 3rd August and completed on the 22nd August, 1928. The work has been thoroughly inspected and has been found to be left in satisfactory condition. Mr. James S. Gregory, the contractor, has executed the work to my satisfaction and in accordance with the terms and spirit of the contract. I find that he is entitled to receive payment for the removal of 11.134.9 cubic yards, scow measurement, class B, at 65 cents, a total of $7,237.69.
Youirs obediently,
Geoffrey Stead,
District Engineer.
The engineer has furnished a plan which I shall be glad to show to my hon. friend. This plan shows that the work was done around the inside and that there is a certain amount of work to be done additional to what was authorized and for which he suggests that he would ask for an estimate. However, no request for an estimate has been received, but I am sure that part of that work can be done out of the general vote.

I hope that will be sufficient. I am sure that the desire of the minister is to have the work carried out so that the result will be satisfactory, and I would ask him to request the engineer to look over that area again and consult with the people in the neighbourhood. There was a certain amount of dredging done but the work is of little value. Perhaps the additional work may correct that, but I think

Supply-Harbour's and Rivers-N.B.
it would be well if the minister would instruct the engineer to interview the people who are using this shelter and obtain their views on the situation.

When we found that we did not have the additional request which the engineer had anticipated making, we issued instructions that a report be made as to what work will be required this year and as to whether or not it can be done out of the general vote. The hon. member is evidently under a misapprehension in thinking that because only S7,312.50 was spent last year out of an appropriation of $11,300, the work was not completed. The appropriation of $11,300 was based on a cost of $1 per yard for 11,250 yards, whereas the work was actually done at a cost of 65 cents per yard. The report from the engineer, which I take to be correct, shows that the work was well done.

That is not the view of the people who are trying to make use of this shelter, and I think that practical experience in a case of this kind is a very valuable test. I am under no misapprehension, as the minister thinks, because I was not considering the amount of money which was spent; my point is that the dredging has not been done in such a manner as to make the shelter suitable and available for the purposes intended. I am basing my views on the knowledge and experience of the men of the locality, who can give a very valuable, practical expression of opinion. I do not, however, want to say too much now, because I really think the minister intends to have something done. I would ask that, apart from the engineer's opinion and some soundings that have been taken, he consult with the men of the locality. They inform me that the work has not been done in accordance with the conditions of the locality so as to make it a serviceable, safe refuge.
Would my hon. friend mention anybody in the locality with whom he would suggest that I confer?
It is about a year since the people interested spoke to me in regard to the matter. I cannot give the names offhand, but I will look into it.

My hon. friend and I
are endeavouring to arrive at the same goal; we want this work properly done. My information is as I have given it. If there is a complaint, none has come to the department. The only statement the department has is the report showing that the work not only is satisfactory, but has been done at a very low price. If my hon. friend will give me the
name of anybody he would like the engineer to confer with when he visits the locality,
I shall be glad to have him do so.

The people complained
to me, and I suppose when they did so they were depending upon me to bring the matter to the attention of the department, as I have done. It may take a few days but I shall be pleased to get some names and forward them to the minister.
Has the department dredged out the harbour and left a shoal outside guarding it?
What my hon. friend suggests is that further work be done around the edges. It is the work around the edges that, it is stated, has not been completed.

It is not quite that.
They say, first that the dredging has not gone near enough to the pier so that at low tide vessels cannot remain near the pier; and, second, that the dredging is being done in an irregular way so that there are hillocks through this space. If a boat happens to be anchored on the top of a hillock, it may turn over when the tide goes down.

Unfortunately I was not
in the house when the item with respect to Escuminac was under consideration. I think it was some days ago that it was under discussion, and I have not been able to find it in Hansard. I should like to know what is the situation at Escuminac. It may be recalled that this work was started, I think as long ago as 1924-25, and that we have been since then making annual votes of about $50,000. This year I notice an amount of $40,000 is being required, and I should like to know whether this completes the work or just where we stand. My information is that what was predicted in the house some years ago has actually happened, namely, that no breakwater can be built at that point and remain there because of ice conditions. I have information now to the effect that the ice has actually lifted the works; that they are more or less of a wreck, and that the contractors are greatly exercised as to who is to bear the loss. Would the minister give a comprehensive statement as to the situation?

This amount is required
to complete the work now under contract.

That is only the part
under contract. Of course this has been built, as the minister knows, in sections, one contract for each section. How much more is to be required in addition to this $40,000 to complete the whole work as projected? My recollection is that the minister's colleague,
2380	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.B.
the Minister of Health, who was Minister of Public Works at the time the project was undertaken, stated that this work was to cost a quarter of a million dollars. Nearly all, if not all, of that amount must have been voted by the house. That is the first point I should like to have elucidated.

My hon. friend is quite right in stating that the work was to be done in sections. The last section is the one for which this $40,000 is required; this will complete the contract for that section. Of this amount, $23,000 is a revote. There is no appropriation at the present time for any further section or for any further portion.
How many more units are to be built in order to complete the whole project which, I understand, originally consisted of five different units?
The original project evidently contemplated doing eventually all that is shown in red and yellow on the map that I have under my hand. My hon. friend has no doubt seen it.
I am familiar with it.

The parts marked in red on the map have been contracted for, and this is to complete the last part of what is marked in red.
. Mr. HANSON: Contracted for?

Yes; they were thought to be the most urgent. No contract has so far oeen entered into for the balance, and no estimate has been inserted for it. The work <hat has been done is the work that it was thought should be done first. As to how soon afterwards the balance will follow is a matter for future consideration.

I quite agree. I should like to know how much, including this appropriation, will 'be expended, and also how much money will be required, according to the engineer's estimate, to build the portion which has not yet been contracted for?
We have no estimate for the cost of the balance. The cost of this last section is $69,000.

Would that be the total expenditure to date, including the $40,000? There is something obviously wrong about that, because we have voted several sums of $50,000 for this project, with all due respect to the minister, I think his information is incomplete.

I have not under my hand the total expenditure in that vicinity. AH I
I Mr. Hanson.]
can say is that the present contract is $61,729 and the probable total cost of the work as shown by the details I have under my hand is as follows:
Amount of contract	$61,729
Inspection, contingencies, etc.. ..	7,271
Total.,	$69,000
That is Obviously for only one unit.

Perhaps my hon. friend will permit me just for one moment. In 192627, 310 feet of this breakwater was built under contract with the Burpee Construction Company, and the amount of the final expenditure was $44,672.56. With the $69,000 that will make about $113,000.

Obviously that is not the
whole story. There was $50,000 voted by this house prior to the general election of 1925 as a direct consequence of a 'bargain which took place before a by-election held in that county about the year 1923. I am giving this information to the minister because he was not in the department then, but the deputy minister knows the facts.
My hon. friend will readily understand that I know nothing about any bargain that took place in any by-election or in any general election.

I would like to know how much this project has cost the country so far, and how much it will cost when completed. I venture to suggest that the figures will be very startling. In addition, predictions were made which have already been fulfilled that no breakwater would ever stand the ice conditions at thaJt point. I made a sporting offer to the Minister of Public Works of that day, the Hon. Doctor King, that if he would get a statement over the signature of Mr. Gray, who was then the district engineer in the city of St. John, that the structure proposed by the government would stand the ice conditions, there would be no opposition to the vote from this side of the house-from me at all events, because I realize that the fishermen require a shelter-but the minister was never able to get that undertaking. The prediction made by those who knew the conditions has been amply fulfilled. The ice has lifted up part of the work that has already been completed, and I want to know what the government are going to do about it. Are they going to make the contractor suffer the loss that has been sustained by reason of these ice conditions, or will the government sustain the loss? In my humble opinion it is not fair to put the loss on the contractor, because the government engineers and departmental officers 'had been fully

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.B.
warned about the ice conditions before the vote was ever passed and, before the project was undertaken.
What is the whole project estimated to cost?
I remember distinctly that prior to the federal election of 1925 the then Minister of Public Works, the Hon. Doctor King, estimated that it would cost 8250,000. The work was started in units estimated to cost 850,000 each, and the separate units were proceeded with year after year. I do not recall just how much work was done, but it is apparent from the minister's figures that he has not the whole data before him. I am satisfied that more than two units have been completed.
I would like an expression from the minister with respect to the ice conditions to which I have referred. The only excuse that could be given for not making a complete statement would be that litigation was pending, in which event I certainly would not want to prejudice the government's case by pressing for a statement here. I do know this, however, that information has reached me that the predictions that were made with regard to this whole project have been already fulfilled, that the work could never stand the ice conditions in the Northumberland straits or in the gulf of the St. Lawrence, where this work happens to be. That is very unfortunate, but it is nevertheless true. I want it distinctly understood that I am not opposing this vote if it can be demonstrated that the work will stand against the ice conditions 'but if the ice conditions are as I believe them to be, and as I have been informed, then I tell the minister that this is just so much money wasted.

In the first place, I am advised that the total estimated cost was not $250,000 as my hon. friend said, but $200,000. That was some years ago. As to the contract to which my hon. friend refers, where the ice conditions, storms or something of that kind rendered it more difficult for the contractor to perform his work, I think my hon. friend will be one of the first in the house to agree that that is something that cannot always tbe foreseen.
Forewarned is forearmed.

Not necessarily. There are certain things that all the forewarning in the world cannot provide against. The precautions that were taken under these specifications were the precautions that the engineers considered reasonable under the circumstances, and they were carried out. A claim has been made, I understand, and is receiving consideration, but as to what will be done about it, no decision has been made, and I am unable to inform my hon. friend what the decision will be.

I am not going to ask the minister to tell me what the judgment of the department is, but I would point out to him that all these ice conditions were brought to the attention of the department when the project was first announced. The department and its engineers were amply warned from this side of the house that the ice conditions were such that it would be practically impossible to maintain the structure as planned and laid down by the engineers. What was then said is in accordance with what has actually happened. I understand that there has been very considerable damage to the structure by the ice conditions, for which the contractor is in no way responsible and for which he should not suffer. In any decision which the minister may arrive at, I would like to assure him that if the facts are as I understand them, there will be no criticism from me at all events-I am speaking only for myself-provided the contractor is treated fairly and squarely and decently, and provided the minister does not load on the contractor the cost of the damage occasioned by the ice conditions, unless it can be shown that he was guilty of negligence or malfeasance in the execution of his contract. I would ask the minister to give this matter his attention, because this work will run into a quarter of a million dollars before it is done if the whole work is completed. That is a large sum of money to pay for a fishermen s shelter. If it were a matter of $15,000 or $25,000, it would not be so much, but this is a quarter of a million dollars of the taxpayers money.
To win a by-election.

Yes, the vote was certainly made for the purpose of influencing a by-election as far back as 1923 or 1924. There is no doubt about that; this certainly is the payment of an election debt. But I am not so much concerned about that, because all that is over and past long ago, and we are dealing now with things as they are. I repeat that this large expenditure should not be gone on with, much as this shelter may be needed by the limited number of fishermen to whom it will be available, unless the government is absolutely certain, on the best engineering advice it can obtain, that the conditions to which I have referred will not recur. They have occurred, and that is justification enough for the attitude that has been taken on this side of the house in regard to this vote in recent years. I ask the minister to look into the matter personally before he spends one dollar of this money. May I say I am not interested in the contractor at present, for he
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.B.

has passed his responsibility on to the subcontractor. Nor am I personally interested in the subcontractor-he is not a political supporter of mine, he is a supporter of the government. I know him; he is all right, he is a decent fellow. I want him to have fair play in the settlement of any claims of his which may now be pending before the department in relation to damage done by reason of ice conditions. That is as far as I wish to go.
I do not want to prolong the discussion,-
I do not either.

-and I do not propose to get into an argument with my hon. friend. He is much more familiar with local conditions and with what took place there in connection with the elections than I am. But if his prophecy and the prophecy of his friends was a warning against something that was going to happen as a result of ice conditions-I take it he agrees to that; he nods his head1-then his prophecy has not been fulfilled, because the claim made by the contractor, if my information is correct, is that the damage is not in any way due to ice conditions, but rather to storms.
I may be all wrong, then.

This "I told you so" may be so easily stretched to cover something that never was intended originally that I do not want to leave my hon. friend under misapprehension any longer. With regard to the claim of the contractor, and that is always a difficult matter for the man in Charge of the department, I make no promise-my hon. friend will readily understand that I cannot- as to what will happen to that contra.etor; but I hope when he gets through that he and the people whose money we are spending will both feel that the fair thing 'has been done in the matter.
That is fair enough.

Item agreed to.
White Head-dredging, $20,500.
Is this White Head island in the county of Charlotte? There are a good many White Heads, you know.
I understand it is in the county of Charlotte.
Are there two items in respect of the same White Head?
Yes. One is dredging and the other a breakwater.
How many yards of material are intended to be moved in this dredging? And is this re-dredging; has it ever been done before by the government?

The first item, $20,500, is asked to be provided towards dredging a channel 100 feet wide extending shorewards from low water at ordinary spring tides, about 725 feet, and a basin in front of the public Wharf about 200 to 250 feet wide and 200 to 300 feet long, to low water ordinary spring tides. It is contemplated that it will be necessary to remove 27,000 cubic yards of sand and gravel at $1.50 per cubic yard at an estimated cost of $40,500. The next is a breakwater at Gull Cove. The amount of $10,000 is required to construct a breakwater 153 feet long, and from 17 to 25 feet wide, for the protection of the 28 motor fishing boats employed in the cove.
I have no doubt the work is required. Has the channel ever been dredged before? I think the minister will find that years ago it was. Perhaps he has not the information before him.
I have not the information.

I think the estimated cost of $1.50 is very high, unless there is rock there, which I do not think there is. For the information of the committee I would point out that this is an isolated island out in the bay of Fundy containing a fishing settlement. They have a great many weather conditions to contend with, and I would be the last one to deny them the facilities they ought to have if they are to carry on their work and be protected from storms. But $1.50 for that dredging is not what I should like to pay for it on a commercial basis. I hope the minister will keep that in mind when having the work done. Is it to be done by the government's own dredges or by Mr. Gregory's?
By contract.
It will go to Mr. Gregory then.
To the lowest tenderer.
He is the only man who is in the business in St. John.
There is the St. John Dry Dock and Shipbuilding Company.
I am not sure that they are in the dredging business now.
Yes, they are.
Perhaps it is just recently.
My hon. friend can rest assured that the same care will be taken to see that this is done at a reasonable cost as is exercised in all cases.

That is the only warning I would give the minister. I may say that the great rise and fall of the tide there is an important factor in the cost of dredging, but even then I have no doubt the work can be done for less than $1.50.
If somebody tenders for less than that he will get the work.

Item agreed to.
Woodward's Cove-Breakwater	extension,

Before the New Brunswick items are carried I wish to call the minister's attention to the necessity for some dredging in the river St. John at the Oromocto shoals, nine miles below the city of Fredericton in my Constituency. The soil is alluvial and rapidly fills in, and there has been no dredging done in the locality since previous to the war,
I think 1912. These shoals form bars which at low water in the summer season render navigation very difficult. There is a daily steamboat running there, and at times she finds it pretty difficult to navigate. Has the minister before him in his records any recommendation with respect to dredging on the Oromocto shoals? I have not made any formal representations to the minister or to his department because I find usually they do not pay much attention to me in that respect.
You are entirely wrong.

They are always very
courteous, but I never get any action, so I have concluded it is not worth while. But I do now very seriously urge upon the minister the necessity and desirability of having such work done on the Oromocto shoals during this present season. Wharfage accommodation has been requested by the residents of the locality and by the Clarke Steamship Company^ for a number of years to provide for growing traffic which is at present greatly handicapped. I am not the Minister of Public Works but I might give a short explanation with regard to this item. Cabano is a big place on the shore of Temiscouata lake, which is 27 miles long and over a mile wide. On the other side of lake Temiscouata there is a farm settlement called Squatek, which consists of 700 or 800 people. A big mill has been erected at Cabano by the Fraser Company, which cuts the wood on the eastern shore of the lake.
For which company is this wood cut?
I do not know, but I do know that my hon. friend from York-Sun-bury is the attorney for the company.

The company does not use this wharf at all; the company builds its own wharves and does not ask the government for help. This is a public wharf for the good of the community. I am not objecting to the item, but I want to know if any steamships operate on that lake. I have been there a good many times without seeing any steamships, although I understand a ferry operates across that lake, which is long and narrow as my hon. friend has said.
It is also very deep.

And I presume this amount is intended to repair that wharf. In connection with the whole situation on the Baie des Chaleurs, would the minister tell us whether the dredging of the harbour at Campbellton and the other necessary dredging between Campbellton and Cross Point was completed last year? This is a large shipping point both for exports and imports.

Of course my hon. friend
is aware of the item for Campbellton in the New Brunswick list.

I was not here when that
item was passed, and I would like to know if that is the estimate of what is required to complete the dredging at Campbellton or whether that is what is to be done this year.

That is all that will be
done this year.

I would like to point out that there is a very substantial development in that part of the province, with a large paper mill being erected at Dalhousie and a very large sulphite pulp mill being erected two miles above the town of Campbellton. A very large amount of supplies will be brought in through Campbellton and it will be the point of shipment by water for perhaps eight months of the year if these companies utilize water transportation, so I think the government should do that dredging at Campbellton this year. It has been requested for quite a long time, and now it is really required; this is practically the only point in the province where there is any large development going on. This is one case where an expenditure of this kind can be fully justified and I submit that the work should be done now and not carried out piecemeal. That is my judgment in the matter and I would like to see the department give attention to this request that the dredging at Campbellton be completed at once. The officers of the department will tell the minister that this is the point of shipment for millions of feet of lumber during the open season and difficulty has been experienced in getting the ships to the piers by reason of the .fact that the river fills in the channel, which must naturally recur from time to time be-

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
cause of the very nature of the river and of the deposits which are brought down annually. I hope the minister will give attention to this request.

I can only say that at

Yes, a good deal was done last year. This $13,600 is a revote because we spent only $16,628 last year out of an appropriation of $30,000.

I would like to explain the situation at Cross Point. This is the most important wharf in my constituency due to the fact that all the traffic between Campbell-ton and Cross Point passes over this wharf. I think over five or six thousand automobiles passed over this wharf last year. The wharf was erected a long time ago-in 1904-and it was proposed to erect an interprovincial bridge at that point. The government of New Brunswick has undertaken to pay its share, the government of Canada is to pay one-third and we are waiting for the government of the Province of Quebec to agree to pay their third of the cost of the bridge. It is estimated that the bridge over the Restigouche river will cost about a million dollars; it will be very important work and is badly needed. Of course the wharf at Cross Point will be retained because there is very heavy traffic at that point. Ohampoux Brothers used to have a large mill at Restigouche but it was sold to the International Paper Company. The Madawaska corporation has purchased or leased this mill for four or five years and this year will conduct very extensive operations on the Mata-pedia and Restigouche rivers. I am in accord with the member for York-Sumbury when he says that Campbellton is the most important port in northern New Brunswick. An extensive development is going on at Dalhousie where the International Paper Company are erecting a huge pulp mill, and another mill is to be erected at Athol. In view of the operations being carried on at Campbellton, and in view of the intended operations at Dalhousie and Restigouche, I am sure the minister should give this matter more than passing attention and see that facilities are granted to this part of the country, which includes territory in both provinces, so that the trade may be carried on.

Where?
At Campbellton and Cross Point. It is all the same thing.

Donnacona - harbour improvements 

 The Donnacona Paper Oo. to contribute one-third of cost, $50,000.

I think this vote requires considerable explanation.

This amount is required to go toward the construction of a long wharf oult to deep water in the St. Lawrenoe river, mainly for the shipment of newsprint, pulp, roofing and agricultural products. The Donnacona Paper Company has been urging these harbour improvements for a number of years, and several schemes have been studied. This wharf will also be used as a coaling station and general operating base for the government ice-breakers and will be available as a shelter for river craft between Cap Rouge and Pointe Platon. It is claimed that this structure will hold the ice and .prevent jamming at Ca,p Rouge, thus preventing the disastrous floods from Cap Rouge to Sorel. The whole work will be very expensive, and it looks as if the total would run into the vicinity of a million dollars, to be divided between the company and the government. The following letter has been received from the chief engineer of the province of Quebec:
A letter has been received from the Acting Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries enclosing copy of memorandum, dated 12th April, 1929, from Mr. N. B. McLean, of the river St. Lawrence ship channel engineering staff which deals with the points raised as to the influence of this proposed structure.
Mr. McLean is of the opinion that the wharf would not interfere with traffic or ice conditions;
(2)	That the wharf would hold a large section of batture ice in place, preventing it floating off during the high water to jam later at Cap Rouge;
(3)	That the wharf would make a place of shelter far ice-breakers and commercial vessels. At present when ice-breakers are working at Portneuf, it is necessary to shelter in the batture ice, which is not always safe.
In order that the wharf may be of the greatest advantage to ice-breakers and commercial vessels, Mr. McLean suggests that the outer end of the wharf be built out to the 30-foot contour line shown on the chart, copy of which he attaches. He further suggests a
berth 500 feet in length, dredged to not less than 25 feet, should be provided on the upper and lower sides of the wharf inside the head-block, and that the depth at the outer face of the headbloek be not less than 25 feet, all depths at low water.
The district engineer in his report calls attention to the fact that Donnacona is situated on the river Jacques Cartier on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river, in the county of Quebec West. Previous to 1911, Donnacona consisted of timber and farm lands; now it is one of the most important pulp and paper centres of the province of Quebec. In 1912 a sixty-ton newsprint paper mill was erected by the Donnacona Pulp and Paper Company, with a 60-ton groundwood pulp mill and a 30-iton sulphite paper mill, giving employment to 800 men. Since then the company has increased its plant so as to have a daily production of 220 tons of newsprint 200 tons of groundwood pulp, and 60 tons ol sulphite pulp, giving employment to about 1,600 men. The company has not yet completed its program of extension and if necessary accommodation by navigation is provided at Donnacona. it is the intention of the company to double the capacity of its mill, to produce at least 500 tons of newsprint per day, meaning an additional population of about 5,000 inhabitants. The company owns and operates another groundwood pulp mill at Pont Rouge, .producing about 5,000 tons per year.

Perhaps I should be the last to rise in the house to defend any project initiated by the Price Brothers company. The Donnacona Paper Company belongs to Price Brothers, and for many years members of the Price family have been in distinct and energetic antagonism to the principles which I represent in the constituency for which I sit in this house. But at the same time, common justice compels me to say that in this case at any rate there is a good deal to be said in favour of the passing of the item. I do not think it is intended to go on with any further newsprint production. The hon. member for York-Sunbury was, I think, quite right in saying that no newsprint company at the present time wishes or would be allowed to increase the production of newsprint, but I understand there is to be a mill utilized for the purpose of using the waste products, slabs, et cetera, of some of the other mills. I am not quite sure what the product is. It is a species of fibre board, but I do not think it is along the lines of insulex and other fibre boards that are being made. It is proposed to bring the waste material from other mills belonging to Price Brothers on the St. Lawrence river and 	-
rivers in the north country to Donnacona as ' much as possible by water and to export the finished product by water to the old country. That, I understand, is the project which the company has laid before the minister and which it intends to carry out. If such be the case, there will be no question of taking away tonnage from either the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific.
Is this a settled policy adopted by the government that they will provide large amounts for wharves and repairs provided that some industry contributes one-third?

Every case has to stand or fall on its own merits. For years this practice has been followed with a view to encouraging industries which perhaps would not come here at all or would not go on with the development which they contemplate unless the government were sympathetic in regard to wharfage facilities and dredging.

Last year the
estimates contained one or two items of the same nature and evidently they have been dropped.
They were not gone on with because the project had not reached the point where we were satisfied that it was going on this year. For that reason they were dropped.
Does the department get any security for the performance by the company of its promise to pay?
We take a guarantee bond from them.
A company bond?
Yes.

Procedure Respecting Divorce
the sponsors of the bills prepared to answer a few questions which may be asked, and one question I have wanted to emphasize is whether or not children are involved and, if so, whether those children are being cared for. True, the Minister of Justice informed us that it is noit within the competence of parliament to grant the custody or demand the maintenance of the children, but even if that be so under the existing interpretation of the British North America Act I still say it is within the competence of parliament to refuse to grant a divorce until such time as the children are cared for, and I think I am quite within my rights in asking this question. I know we cannot do very much in these cases, but if an outstanding case is brought forward where children are being neglected, we might refer that case back to the committee for reconsideration.
In the meantime I want to emphasize the fact that in this house we are occupying a most anomalous position. As far as the state is concerned the chief reason why marriage is recognized is that there may be care for the family, yet here we are in a position where we cannot give effect to this principle which lies at the very root of marriage. That sort of thing should not and cannot continue very long. That we should recognize the union of two people and yet not be in a position to see that their offspring are cared for is hard to understand. Judging from the communications which have been coming to me from different quarters it is only beginning to dawn upon the people of Canada what an outrage has been perpetrated here throughout the years, and I do not think society as a whole will agree to permit a procedure to continue whereby we simply throw the children on the streets. I think the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is of extreme importance. I was not here the other day when the Minister of Justice gave his opinion with regard to the jurisdiction of this house with respect to what I might call the civil consequences or results of a divorce granted by this house, but I think that opinion is incontrovertible, and it exemplifies the absurdity of the whole situation. Of course, the principle of divorce is just as bad in the case of married people without children. But as I have already stated my position in that regard, I need not go over it again.
But when it comes to the question of children I know of no civilized and so-called Christian country on earth where the dissolution of marriage or the separation of married people, what we call in French, separation de corps, which is allowed in the province of Quebec,-you call it in English, separation a mensa et thoro-nowhere is it allowed without the court giving its decision with regard to the children, deciding which of the separated parties, the father or the mother, shall have the custody of the children and what means shall be taken to provide for their maintenance. That is done everywhere. I know of no country, whether it be the United States, Engjand, France, Belgium, Germany or any other country the legislation of which I know anything about, which does not always look

Procedure Respecting Divorce
alter the children. It is essential; it is the duty of the state, as represented by the jurisdiction created by the government, to adjudicate upon such matters, to consider what will become of the children. The responsibility of the state towards the child is greater than its responsibility towards the man and woman who cannot agree to live together and are asking for a separation. If it is the decided opinion of the government, or of the Minister of Justice, who is the legal adviser of the government, that this parliament is not em,powered judicially or constitutionally to carry out its primary duty towards the child born of a marriage dissolved by this parliament, then this parliament has not the moral right to pronounce any divorce in oases where there are children, until and unless some means have been found to provide for the children, as they are provided for by regular courts of justice in any country where such separations or divorces are granted. This only shows that the problem cannot be solved until we have amended the constitution in such a manner that the power which has jurisdiction over the marriage will have the whole jurisdiction. So Jong as we exercise one jurisdiction here and the other jurisdiction is exercised by another power over which we have no control, we will never get satisfaction. Some harm may be done in cases where only two individuals, the parties to the marriage contract, are concerned, but it is much more strongly exemplified where there are Children.
At times I hear some suppressed laughter in the house, but I would ask the members of this house to remember that this is one of the most serious questions before the country. It is concerning the thoughtful people of Canada much more than thoughtless people seem to imagine. Not very long ago the Anglican synod-quite a respectable body, I think-gathered and expressed its opinion with regard to this matter. Two of its most respected and high placed members, the Bishop of Ottawa and one of his colleagues, have issued a document which is one of the most comprehensive pronouncements on this question I have read for a long time. They called the attention not only of the members of their own church but of all thoughtful Canadians to the threat to the country arising from the disquieting increase in divorces from year to year. If that is a threat in itself, surely it is a much greater threat when we dissolve a family and, as the member for Winnipeg North Centre has just said, throw the children on the street and leave it to haphazard to decide how they will be taken care of, to which of the parents they will be given, whether to the worthy one or to the the unworthy one.
I am not a believer in the doctrine of the state taking the place of the parents in the matter of education, whether it is family education or school education; but when the state takes upon itself the responsibility of breaking the family tie, surely it should do something for the preservation of those members of the family who are incapable, either morally, physically or legally, of protecting themselves. We decide that the marriage is dissolved, the man goes where he likes and the woman does what she wishes, and no provision is made for the children; we wash our hands of all responsibility towards the children. This is an extremely serious aspect of the question, apart from all the circumstances surrounding it. When we consider the basic principle of the indissolubility of marriage, we must not forget that this other principle is just as important.
I assume that it will take some process of education to bring home to the people of the country a realization of the harm which was done at the time of confederation with regard to divorce. The power which per-'orms the operation of breaking a family tie has now to admit that it is incapable, that it is impotent to perform what is considered in every civilized country as the primary duty of the authority which pronounces divorce-to take care of the children. It seems to me that the least we could do would be to say that before a divorce is granted, in cases where there are children concerned, such procedure should take place as was spoken of a moment ago by the member for Parkdale. The hon. member mentioned a case where a court of justice in Ontario had decided, before application for divorce was made, as to whom the child should be given and as to the allowance to be paid to the mother or the father, as the case may be, for the maintenance of that child. I say that it is essential that no petition for a divorce should be received by this parliament in cases where children are concerned until such procedure has taken place before a regular court of justice. That seems to me to be the least we could do. Finding out that we cannot ourselves exercise that duty, we should say to the parties who ask for divorce, " In case you have children you must go before a court of justice and have it decided as to what will become of the children, how they will be taken care of, and to whom they will be given." It seems to me that that is an extremely reasonable proposition, and if we still believe in the necessity of the maintenance of the principle of the family tie, it is about time that we retraced our steps as far as that aspect of the question is concerned. Therefore I think
Procedure Respecting Divorce

that in connection with this bill or any other bill involving children in regard to whom no judicial decision has been obtained in the province in which reside the parties in the case, no such petition should be received, and no such bill should be passed upon. It may be said that this suggestion is late; but it is never too late. Let what amount those parties have deposited be remitted to them; let them put themselves in a proper position in that regard before they ask for divorce from this parliament, and parliament should not grant a divorce until the whole case has been covered as it should be.

This is a case where the mother about nine or ten years ago contracted a filthy disease from her husband. She separated from him; for nine years she has been living apart and supporting her children and she wishes so to continue.

I would like to draw the

The lake is about 90 miles long and most of the traffic from that country passes up and down the lake. I spent about three weeks travelling up and down that country and found that requests had been made that a wharf be placed at MacDonald landing and also at one or two other points along the lake. The Burns Lake board of trade, representing that great district, presented their views on this matter. After obtaining full particulars of these requests I visited Victoria and presented them to Mr. J. P. Forde, the federal engineer, and he promised me that he would send in one of his men to investigate the conditions. I happened to be at Burns Lake when Mr. Forde's engineer came there and I assumed that he had come in at the request of the board of trade at Burns Lake, but I found that he had travelled these thousands of miles at the request of the secretary of the Liberal association at Endalco. The question arises in my mind as to why a federal engineer should be sent in at considerable expense at the request of one man and the request of the main body of the people concerned should be ignored. I have been in this house three years and the more I examine into the Public Works department the more I realize that the sooner it is taken out of the realm of politics the better it will be for the development of Canada. I do not blame the Minister of Public Works as I think the fault lies with the men whose duty it is to present to the minister the needs of these outlying districts. Water transportation is the only means afforded to the people on this lake of transporting their produce to the Francois lake crossing where the ferry is. I contend, Mr. Chairman, that there is the greatest need on Francois lake for at least four wharves. On the opposite side of the lake is MacDonald landing where there is a large agricultural settlement, and they have no means of taking their products down to the lake and over to Burns lake where the railway is. From the Stellato river, where Glenannon is, down to Nadina, a distance of 90 miles, there is not a single wharf on that great inland lake. I have gone to the minto float approach,

ister repeatedly and I have found that he has given me consideration, but the unfortunate thing is that the information he acts upon is from a quarter that I do not believe in nine cases out of ten expresses exactly the needs of that district. May I ask my hon. friend a question? I have no doubt he has followed the interests of British Columbia very carefully. Is he not aware that this year they are getting a much higher percentage of the Public Works appropriation than they have for many years, and they are certainly not getting it in ridings that are not supporters of friends of my hon. friend. I just wanted to know whether my hon. friend knew that.

I am thoroughly familiar
with the conditions. I have been in this house for three years and I know that section of the country very well. In the past three years there has been the greatest neglect in the matter of public works for the Skeena constituency. We are living on the Pacific coast; we have an immense coastline and the main need of the people who are living along that coastline is wharves. I grant that the government has done something this year, but it is a belated gift. There are two great needs in the matter of wharf accommodation along the northern British Columbia coast. A couple of years ago there was in the estimates an item of $40,000 for a new wharf at Stewart. That, however, was taken out of the estimates. Why that was done I am not going to explain, although I could give a veiy good reason. What is the condition of the Stewart wharf to-day? I have before me the results of a four-days visit that I paid last September to Stewart. I took with me the leading citizens of that town in order that they might corroborate what I was writing down in regard to tlie congestion on the government wharf there. I know the minister has in his possession from the federal engineer, and Captain Saunders at Digby, reports regarding the Stewart wharf. Nevertheless the conditions at Stewart to-day are such that it is imperative that the Public Works department build a wharf there. The Premier mine have a practical monopoly upon the government wharf; their ore is passed over it. There is congestion from one end to the other. I found on that wharf tons of machinery that belonged to the Premier mine and that had been lying there for months. I found that when the Canadian National steamers and the Union steamers called there, the congestion was so great with [Mr. Brady.1
all kinds of produce for the Marmot mine, the Premier mine and other places that is was impossible for the passengers to go down by the gangway and with impunity pass to their automobiles to take them to Stewart or to Hyder. The explanations given to me by the federal engineer as well as by Captain Saunders have been contradicted by every captain of the Canadian National and the Union steamships and also by the captains of the ore carriers, such as the Mogul and those boats that take the ore from that place. This is what the captain of one of those steamships said to me: after a wire had been sent to Ottawa ''Your wire is only a joke compared to what you should sent in." In other words, that particular section is the most important mining area in the whole of northern British Columbia. There is the Premier mine, the Big Missouri, the Marmot mines, the Silverado, the Prosperity,-a whole great section which is comparable with anything either in Ontario of Quebec. What happened was this: a new wharf was built by Mr. Crawford for his own special purpose, for coal and other things, and it did not in any way relieve the congestion at the government wharf. When I went there I was told that Crawford's wharf and the wharf built by the Premier at the Marmot, were able to relieve the congestion on the main Stewart wharf. That is not the case. I do not want to compel the Minister of Public Works to do anything he should not do, but I contend that the most necessary thing in that section to-day is that a wharf should be built at Stewart to meet the requirements of that fast growing mineral area.

When the minister made
the observation that British Columbia was getting somewhat better consideration in this estimate this year than last year, he left the impression that British Columbia generally was getting the benefit of that increase.

that we were getting a larger appropriation, this year for works of this kind throughout British Columbia as compared with last year. Let me point out that the increase in the vote this year as compared with last year comes in three particular places: There is $100,000 for dredging the north arm of th->
Fraser river. Then there is $300,500 for improvements to the Fraser river, which is $100,500 in excess of last year. Then there is an item of $124,500 for dredging the First

Narrows, so that apart from these votes there is for the rest of the province $742,300, as compared with $774,000 last year. The hon. member for Skeena is certainly correct when he says that a lot of these places in the northern country are not getting the consideration they deserve. I have in the central part of my constituency Quesnel lake, and on the whole of the ninety miles of its shore line there is not a single wharf. Just to clear this matter up, let me say that I am not finding fault with the criticism; I think I would be very unfair did I not express my appreciation of the tone of the criticism that has characterized the passing of these estimates. But I do think it is unfair to the people of the other provinces and to this department for the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Cariboo, in view of these estimates for British Columbia, to get up here and suggest that these estimates for public works are gauged largely by considerations of political patronage. I have taken the trouble to ascertain the percentage of the total appropriation for harbours and rivers that the province of British Columbia has received in past years, and I find that from 1914-15 to 1921-22- those were war years-British Columbia's percentage of the total expenditure was 2.24; from 1922-23 to 1927-28, British Columbia's percentage was 2.41, and for this year her percentage is 3.60 of the total appropriation. I do not think that any hon. gentleman will object to any one item in these estimates if he is fair. I would rather have expected my hon. friend from Skeena, who in season and out of season, every time this committee has sat, has asked for floats at Prince Rupert and has spoken of the great amount of credit he would give to this government and to this department if they saw fit to provide those floats, to express his appreciation now that those floats are provided for in the estimates, but he has never referred to that fact at all. He does not know the percentage of the total appropriations which British Columbia is now getting as compared with what that province usually gets, that its percentage is now half as much again as it has been for many years. There is nothing my hon. friend can say to which I will not give consideration, but I do believe that he tries to seize every opportunity to make a little political capital for 78594-1524
himself and his friends in that part of the country. I would ask him if he thinks it is fair, in view of what these estimates show, or if he thinks he is advancing the interests of Skeena, to make the criticism he made here to-night when not one of those ridings in which these appropriations are being expended is represented by a Liberal.
I did not say that.
The minister said that I was not grateful for what he did.
That is better.

So far as the appropriations in these estimates are concerned, they were essential, not this year, but three years ago, and these necessary works have been kept back all that time. I think I know the reason why. I have stated in this house, and I intend to repeat it until I get what I want, that the public works of this country should be outside the influence of any member of parliament and of any defeated member of parliament. There are great needs in the northern part of British Columbia to be filled of which the Minister of Public Works

is not yet aware. He states that British Columbia's percentage of the total appropriation for this year is 3.60. Does he forget that there has been a wonderful development in northern British Columbia in the last three years?
And in the other provinces too.

I admit that, but I contend that there is an obligation upon the Department of Public Works to provide these wharves and other improvements for that section of the country where the great majority of the people live, not in the interior as in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario, but right on the Pacific ocean. Perhaps I did.

I think you did, sir, because if I had chosen-I did not think it necessary, as it was your duty-I would have thanked you for four or five of those. But, sir, there are many necessary public works in my part of British Columbia not yet provided for. Remember, I am speaking now to the Minister of Public Works. If the minister could get one of his engineers to make a thorough investigation of the needs of that vast constituency, and give him an honest, exact report, he would find that what I have said to-night can be absolutely verified. I will give you an instance, sir. Take Port Clements on Queen Charlotte Island. Port Clements to-day is the centre of the traffic from the south and the east end of the island. The provincial government have built a road whereby the whole of the traffic from east and west moves to Port Clements. Now, I ask the minister to instruct his engineer to proceed there and investigate conditions, and I believe he will find at Port Clements a great need for a new wharf and also for additional protection of the local fleet.
This is the first time that I have been told that anything I say in this house is for the purpose of making political capital. I spent over twenty-eight years of my life in teaching the youth of the empire, and I do not want now to retrace my steps, I do not want now to be placed in the position of being told that I am coming to Ottawa for one purpose only-political capital. I entered into the political world not for that purpose, and I say to the Minister of Public

Works that I have never yet spoken one word in this house nor outside of it, and I hope I never shall, that is not intended for the good of the people and for the good of the country.

If Mr. Chairman, I misunderstood my hon. friend. I am very sorry. The public works engineers who are charged with the responsibility of going all over the country to make reports upon the requests received-and they are numerous and sometimes very difficult to deal with-I believe are making a fair and honest endeavour to send in reports that w'ill best serve the interests of the various parts of the country concerned, and I do not think my hon. friend should have referred to the fact that if our engineers would send in honest and exact reports the department would do something different from what they have done. Our engineers are in a difficult position, they are working very hard, and I believe they are doing their work well.

This is a very important question which has been before the department for some time, and those of us who are well acquainted with the particular trouble on the Fraser river at that point believe that the proper thing to do is to remove the cause. The cause of the erosion of the bank on the north side of the river at Nicomen island has been set forth by the engineer in a letter which I received from the deputy minister on February 1 of this year, in which he says:
After the observations made during last year's freshet, I believe the main cause of the erosion of the south bank of Nicomen island is due to the movement of the deep water channel of the river towards the north. This is being caused by two factors. The first is the cutting of the river into the south bank above McDonald's bar, which has been very severe during the past years, and is still active, even at low water stages of the river. This cutting has formed a very sharp curve of this bank which guides the current during the lower stages of the river over towards Nicomen island more directly than ever before. The second is that the materials from this bank cutting-consisting of gravel and sand from above-mentioned high bank-have been deposited along the northerly side of McDonald's bar, thus extending the bar towards Nicomen island, and naturally pushing the deep water channel over towards the island.
The engineer reported in regard to the matter and action was taken in 1913 along that line. In that year this same engineer, under the same officers of the department, reported favourably on cutting a channel on the south side so that the main body of the river would be carried down and diverted from the Nicomen island side. In answer to a question of mine certain information was given on February 27, as reported at pages 534 and 535 of Hansard. This work was recommended by the present engineer, and the statement appears in Hansard that the object was to divert the current from Nicomen island, where the bank was eroded. This channel, known as the King Edward cut, was proceeded with; it was some 5,600 feet long and 150 feet wide and cost the country $87,225.40. This cut was never completed and therefore there was no relief given, although they came within about 1,600 feet of completing it. In answer to a question as to why tnis work was not completed the reason

given was the high elevation of discharge and also the running ice which endangered the plant.
I waited upon the deputy minister last year in regard to this matter and he informed me that he did not think it good business to do any more dredging at this point, that it was simply throwing money into the river and that the channel had completely filled in. Last October I went to that district and, with some of the residents, proceeded up this channel in a gas boat; and with a 12-foot pole we could not find bottom. I agree that at the upper end there has been some slight filling in, but the channel appeared to be in almost the same condition as when the dredge left it. As I say, we consider it will be good business to complete this work because, as the minister stated, a large amount of money has been expended in order to protect that bank. We are spending this year another $40,000, which will give only temporary protection. In 1927 the engineer pointed out that it was very necessary that the banks of Nicomen island be protected; he said that the bank then was within 100 feet of the dyke built by the provincial government about four years previously. Last year a portion of the dyke was washed out, and in the opinion of some of the provincial engineers and those who reside in that district this work will not stand the heavy freshets. On November 9, 1928, the deputy minister wrote me as follows:
Our efforts to induce the river to follow a cut at this point in the past were expensive and, as you are quite aware, produced no result. While those efforts were well intended the nonsuccess only makes us more hesitant to undertake any further expenditure there.
I would ask the committee how any results could be expected with this channel completely isolated during low and medium water. During the construction of the channel the material was thrown into the centre of the river; a sort of dyke or bar was thus formed and at the east end of the work the gravel is some fifteen feet high.
As I said before, the engineer has been favourable to the completion of this work. He visited this district on March 16, 1927, and I have in my hand a letter which was written the next day by a member of the party who met and accompanied the engineer to that spot. He says.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. 4, to amend and consolidate the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act-Hon. Mr. King-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This bill being
of a technical character, it was decided when it was before the house on a previous occasion to refer it to a special committee. This committee held a number of sittings at which the bill was carefully considered section by
Narcotic iDrug Act

section, and in addition, those who 'are engaged in the legitimate traffic in drugs appeared before the committee and made representations-I refer to representatives of the retail and wholesale druggists. These representatives were also permitted to be in contact and consultation with officers of the department and with the officers of the Justice department who drew the amendments as recommended by the committee. The bill as now presented I think meets the objects and desires of the departmental officers, and I think also clarifies any misunderstanding or doubts that might have existed in the minds of members of the committee or of those engaged in the legitimate traffic. I have an amendment to move to section 6 when we come to it, something that has come up since the committee adjourned. I will explain it when we reach the section.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 and 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Importing or exporting drug without license.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Are we not going to
take up this section clause by clause?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If it is the desire of
the committee, we can take up the subsections separately, but I called section 4.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member for
East Calgary was a member of the special committee, and I think we were agreed on every clause as it went through.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The first subsection deals with the penalties, and there are two features in connection with the penalties to which I objected in the committee and to which I still object. Section 1 provides that upon indictment an offender may be sentenced to imprisonment for any term not exceeding seven years, and in addition, at the discretion of the judge, he may be whipped. I object, first of all, to the practice of whipping. It is a relic of the dark ages when the rack and the thumbscrew were used to torture offenders. Secondly, this subsection does not. fix any maximum penalty. In the case of penalties for any other offence, whether fine or imprisonment, there is a maximum penalty; it must not exceed such-and-such, but in this case there is no maximum penaitj'; it is left open to the judge to sentence a man to one or two or a hundred lashes as he sees fit. I think that is entirely wrong, even if you leave it to the discretion of the judge to order whipping, which, as I say, I look upon as a relic of the dark ages. Again, a 
man may be subjected to the penalty of whipping after a first offence. If you are going to whip at all, which I strongly object to, I do not think it should be inflicted as a penalty for the first offence. Give a man a second chance. I suggested in the special committee that that clause ought to be amended. I do not know how the committee of the whole house feels, but I would move, Mr. Chairman, to amend that subsection so that it will not be left to the discretion of the judge to order whipping.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
will have to submit his amendment in writing.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I know that my
hon. friend from East Calgary took exception in the committee to the penalty of whipping, but the matter was very thoroughly discussed and it was ascertained that whipping is not a new section in this bill, or a new principle applied to this offence. Whipping already was applied at the discretion of the judge where the trafficker gave or sold drugs to a minor. We have extended that principle in order to provide a greater deterrent to those who are engaged in trafficking. From the information I have received from all parts of the Dominion since the bill was in committee, I am satisfied that those who are interested in the curtailment and suppression of this traffic are entirely in sympathy with the provision that whipping be left to the discretion of the judge.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman any criticism of its being unlimited whipping?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is always limited by the judge.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Was the old section in that form? It seems extraordinary. Under this section might not a convicted person be sentenced to be whipped once a week during his imprisonment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In the criminal code it is the same-the judge exercises his discretion.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will the minister except whipping for the first offence?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The reason given in the committee for imposing the penalty of whipping for the first offence was extraordinary.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think the discretion can very well be left to the judge. I am satisfied that for the first offence the judge would not impose the penalty of whipping.

speechtext:

members of the committee object to the section?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have an amendment to move to section 6.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is the section on
which we had so much discussion when the bill was before the house on another occasion?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes. I beg to propose the following amendment as subsection 2 to section 6:
Notwithstanding the provisions of the criminal code, or of any other statute or law, the court shall have no power to impose less than the minimum penalties herein prescribed.
Until recently we have had very little trouble under this section, as we were fortified by a judgment of the appeal court of Ontario that upon trial by indictment and conviction the minimum sentence was three months' imprisonment, and that the judge had no discretion but to impose this sentence. However, in the last week or two, since the bill was reported by the special committee, the appeal court of another province has decided differently, and ruled that under section 1,035 of the criminal code it is within the competence of the magistrate or judge to impose a fine and refrain from imposing imprisonment. Our officer makes this note:
Proceedings by indictment are not taken against a professional man except under the most serious circumstances. As we are thus faced with two conflicting judgments, and as the intent of parliament is obviously that in such serious cases a minimum of three months' imprisonment should be awarded, the matter was discussed with the Department of Justice, who agreed that it would be advisable to place the matter beyond any doubt, and this can best he effected by adding a new subsection.
This is the subsection that I have just moved by way of amendment.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think as the other members of the committee that considered this bill are not present, and this is a decided change in the section, it had better stand.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Then we will go on with the other sections.
Section stands.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Has the minister
taken into consideration such a case as I brought to his attention on a former occasion? A practising physician administered a narcotic drug-I do not know under what circumstances-and a charge was made against him. If some person had not taken up his case that physician might have been whipped.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In such a case the judge would use his discretion. If the accused was found to be a regular trafficker, committing a crime worse than murder, and the judge decided that whipping was proper punishment,
I do not think anyone would abject. But ordinarily professional men are not proceeded against on indictment unless they are found to be really engaged in the drug traffic. The case referred to would not come under this section.
Mr. R.OSS (Kingston): The evidence of the special officer engaged in the case would have been sufficient to render the accused liable to such a punishment, would it not?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Why not? I ask for information.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The judge, exercising his discretion, would see that this did not happen. Some of these matters must be left to the judge; we cannot possibly prescribe for every case.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think the officers employed in the enforcement of this law should be specially qualified. In the case I have referred to they should not have entered such a charge against the doctor. If they are to have full control of these cases as in the past ' we may have some very unfortunate results.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: We have special officers in the department known as enforcement officers under the narcotic acts. Their agents throughout the country are the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the municipal and provincial police.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am quite sure that if they had consulted the municipal or provincial officers they would never have laid such a charge.
